transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Could you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Um, well, I didn't really even want to come in today, to be completely honest. It's just... so, I volunteer with these youth workshops on campus—it's this really great program where we help high school kids from the area with their creative writing and college prep stuff. I've been doing it since last semester, and it takes up a ton of time, but I absolutely love it. Anyway, you have to get this basic medical clearance from student health to participate, which is honestly so bureaucratic and ridiculous, but I went in last week just to get my form signed off. 

And the nurse, or whoever she was, she got really, really hung up on the scale. They told me my weight is too low to clear me for the workshops. Which is so frustrating because I feel completely fine! They were making this huge deal about how the number has kept dropping since my freshman physical, and I guess it has, but... I don't know, to me, it just feels like what naturally happens when I’m focused and really busy. I mean, I have a full course load, plus the volunteering, plus I'm trying to keep my GPA up for grad school eventually, so I'm just running around all day. It makes sense that I wouldn't be holding onto extra pounds, you know? But they absolutely refused to sign the paper and said I had to come see someone here first. So... here I am. I'm just trying to get this whole thing sorted out so I can get back to my kids.
Have you been intentionally trying to lose weight or avoid gaining weight, even if it meant eating less or changing your eating habits?

I mean... "intentionally" is kind of a weird word for it. It’s not like I’m sitting around obsessing over diet magazines or whatever it is they think I’m doing. It’s more about... well, it’s about having a routine that works for me and keeps me focused. Because my schedule is so crazy right now, I actually kind of have to plan my whole day around not really eating. It just takes up too much time, and it makes me feel sluggish when I need to be sharp. 

So, like, my typical day, I’ll just get a large black coffee right before studio—I have this morning prep studio where I organize the materials for the high schoolers—and that coffee is really all I need. It keeps me going. And then later on, if I’m at the campus café with my study group or the other volunteers, I know how people get. They get nosy, and they stare. So if I feel like people are watching me, I’ll maybe buy a salad or something and just take a few little bites of it, just to keep them from making comments and getting in my business. 

But even then, I’m really, really specific about what I’ll even touch. Like, I completely avoid bread. I won't go near it. Or anything oily—the dining halls here just soak everything in oil and heavy sauces, and it’s honestly just unnecessary. If I were to eat something like that, it just... it feels like it would completely undo all the control I’ve worked so incredibly hard for. And I need that control to get through everything I have on my plate right now, with the workshops and my classes. So, I guess I do eat less, and I have strict habits, but it’s really just about keeping my life manageable and feeling disciplined, you know? It's not this big scary thing the health center is making it out to be.
Do you find yourself feeling afraid of gaining weight or becoming fat, even if others might see you as underweight?

I mean... "afraid" almost sounds too mild for what it actually is. It’s more like... well, it’s a total panic. Just the very idea of it. If I even think about the scale going up by a single pound, my heart just starts racing and I can't focus on anything else for the rest of the day. It’s this overwhelming dread. 

Like, if I were to just sit down and eat a quote-unquote "normal" dinner—which, again, is impossible on campus because the dining halls just drown everything in grease and salt—but if I did, or if I accidentally ate something that had butter hidden in it... I would completely lose it. I actually have to interrogate the cafeteria workers sometimes just to make sure they didn't sneak butter into the steamed vegetables, and they roll their eyes at me and act like I'm being such a burden, but I absolutely have to know. Because if I eat that, if I gain even a tiny bit of weight, it feels like everyone will instantly be able to see it on me. They’ll look at me and they'll just know that I’ve completely lost my discipline. 

And my discipline is basically the only thing holding my life together right now. It’s what makes me good at my classes, it’s what makes me reliable for the youth workshops. If I gain weight, it’s like walking around with a giant neon sign on my forehead that says I’m lazy, that I gave up, that I can't even control my own daily choices. The other volunteers, the high school kids, my professors... they all see me as the one who has everything perfectly organized and under control. If I get soft, they're going to see that I'm slipping and that I'm not who they think I am. So, I don't really care if the health center nurse thinks I look underweight, because she doesn't know my life or what I have to do to keep it all running. To me, the thought of putting on even one pound is just... it's absolutely terrifying. It would ruin everything I've worked so hard to maintain.
Have you ever made yourself vomit, used laxatives or diuretics, or exercised excessively to control your weight or keep from gaining it back?

Oh, God, no. No, I would never do any of that. Throwing up? That just seems so... I don't know, chaotic? And messy. The whole point of how I manage my life is about keeping things neat and completely under control. If I were making myself sick, I'd feel like I was totally spiraling. Plus, honestly, where would I even find the privacy for that? I live in a dorm with communal bathrooms, and the walls are paper-thin. The girls on my floor are already so incredibly nosy and always in each other's business. If I were in there getting sick, it would turn into this massive dramatic situation, and I just do not have the time or the energy to deal with dorm drama on top of my course load. I just bypass the whole issue by not eating the things that would make me want to do that in the first place. 

And pills, like laxatives or water pills or whatever... absolutely not. That just sounds like a complete nightmare for my schedule. Like I was saying before, I have the youth workshops, I have my morning prep studio, I'm in back-to-back seminars most afternoons... I can't be worrying about, you know, suddenly needing to run to the restroom in the middle of helping a high schooler edit their college essay. That would be so unprofessional and humiliating. I need my body to just run efficiently and predictably on exactly what I give it. I can't deal with any surprises like that. 

And as for exercising... I mean, I see people at the campus rec center who just look so sweaty and frantic, running on treadmills for hours on end, and I just don't do that. For one thing, I literally don't have the time. My schedule is packed from six in the morning until midnight. I walk a ton, obviously, because our campus is huge and I'm constantly rushing back and forth between the library and the student center and my classes, but I'm not doing crazy, punishing workouts. I just don't need to. My routine with managing my intake is perfectly fine on its own. It works. Doing all those other extreme things... to me, that just seems like what people do when they mess up and lose control of their eating, and they have to fix it. But I have the discipline to just not mess up.

latest_inference.note: The patient denies engaging in purging behaviors, such as vomiting, laxative use, or diuretics, which rules out F50.02 (Anorexia Nervosa, purging type). The patient also does not meet criteria for F50.00 (Anorexia Nervosa, restricting type) as the focus is more on control and discipline rather than a drive for thinness. The predominant feature is restriction without purging, aligning with F50.01 (Anorexia Nervosa, restricting type).
